standards.statement: Develop an understanding of how to use and create a timeline.
Sequence three events using a simple timeline such as events in the school day and at home.

Examine primary sources, such as letters, photographs or paintings.
Compare children and families of today with those in the past.
Recognize items from the present and the past.
Recognize the importance of celebrations and national holidays as a way of remembering and honoring people, events, and our nation's ethnic heritage.
Identify national holidays and celebrations that honor people or events.
Compare our nation's holidays with holidays of other countries' cultures.
Recognize the similarities and differences between holidays in our nation and other cultures.
Listen to and retell stories about people in the past who have shown character ideals and principles including honesty, courage, and responsibility.
Identify an act of bravery or honesty in stories.
Recognize the importance of U.S. symbols.
Identify the pledge of allegiance.
Use words and phrases related to chronology and time to explain how things change and to sequentially order events that have occurred in school.
Recognize events that occur in the day and the night.
Explain that calendars represent days of the week and months of the year.
Recognize a calendar.
Recognize African American inventors and explorers (i.e., Lonnie Johnson [inventor], Mae C. Jemison, George Washington Carver).
Recognize African American inventors or explorers (i.e., Lonnie Johnson [inventor], Mae C. Jemison, George Washington Carver).
Identify the purpose of rules and laws in the home and school.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will define rules as standards of responsible behavior (e.g., rules for home and school). Clarification 2: Students will define laws as a system of rules intended to protect people and property that are created and enforced by government (e.g., speed limit). Clarification 3: Students will identify what can happen without rules and laws.

standards.statement: Recognize an example of a rule (home and school) or law (government).
Identify people who have the authority and power to make and enforce rules and laws.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify authority figures in their school and community including, but not limited to, parents, teachers, and law enforcement officers.

standards.statement: Recognize people who have authority and make rules.
Describe and demonstrate the characteristics of being a responsible citizen.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify examples of responsible citizenship. Clarification 2: Students will demonstrate that conflicts can be resolved in ways that are consistent with being a responsible citizen. Clarification 3: Students will explain why it is important to take responsibility for one’s actions.

standards.statement: Demonstrate a characteristic of being a responsible citizen in the classroom.
Describe ways for groups to make decisions.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will practice decision-making in small and large groups through voting, taking turns, class meetings, and discussion. Clarification 2: Students will identify examples of responsible decisions.

standards.statement: Recognize a way to make a decision, such as raising hands or taking turns.
Define patriotism as the allegiance to one’s country.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify patriotic holidays and observances (e.g., American Founders Month, Celebrate Freedom Week, Constitution Day, Independence Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Medal of Honor Day, Memorial Day, Patriot Day, Veterans Day). Clarification 2: Students will recognize that the Pledge of Allegiance is an oath that affirms American values and freedom. Clarification 3: Students will identify “I pledge allegiance to the flag of the United States of America and to the republic for which it stands, one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty, and justice for all” as the Pledge of Allegiance.

standards.statement: Students will recognize "I pledge allegiance to the flag of the United States of America and to the republic for which it stands, one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all" as the Pledge of Allegiance.
Recognize symbols that represent the United States.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize the American flag, the bald eagle, and the U.S. President as symbols that represent the United States.

standards.statement: Identify the United States flag.
Recognize symbols that represent Florida.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize Florida’s state flag and state nickname, “The Sunshine State,” as symbols that represent the state.

standards.statement: Identify a Florida symbol.
Describe different kinds of jobs that people do and the tools or equipment used.
standards.remarks: Examples are community helpers, firefighter and fire truck).

standards.statement: Identify school and community workers.
Recognize that United States currency comes in different forms.
standards.remarks: Examples are coins and bills.

standards.statement: Recognize an example of money.
Recognize that people work to earn money to buy things they need or want.
Recognize that people use money to buy things.
Identify the difference between basic needs and wants.
standards.remarks: Examples ofneeds areclothing and shelter and examples of wants are video games and toys.

standards.statement: Recognize basic needs.
Describe the relative location of people, places, and things by using positional words.
standards.remarks: Examples are near/far; above/below, left/right and behind/front.

standards.statement: Identify the relative location of an object by using positional words.
Explain that maps and globes help to locate different places and that globes are a model of the Earth.
Recognize a map as a drawing of a place.
Identify cardinal directions (north, south, east, west).
Track movement in different directions on a map.
Differentiate land and water features on simple maps and globes.
standards.remarks: Examples are blue is water and green/brown is land.

standards.statement: Identify land and water on a simple map or globe.
Locate and describe places in the school and community.
standards.remarks: Examples are the cafeteria, library, office, restrooms, and classroom.

standards.statement: Identify a place in the classroom or school.
Know one’s own phone number, street address, city, or town and that Florida is the state in which the student lives.
Identify the city or town one lives in, and that Florida is the state in which the student lives.
Identify basic landforms.
standards.remarks: Examples are hills, forests, wetlands, and coasts.

standards.statement: Recognize basic landforms.
Identify basic bodies of water.
standards.remarks: Examples are rivers, lakes, oceans, and gulfs.

standards.statement: Recognize basic bodies of water.
Describe and give examples of seasonal weather changes and illustrate how weather affects people and the environment.
Recognize types of weather and a way weather affects people.
Develop an understanding of a primary source.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to, pictures, letters, audio/video recordings, and other artifacts.

standards.statement: Identify a primary source.
Understand how to use the media center and other sources to find answers to questions about a historical topic.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,databases, audio orvideo recordings, and books.

standards.statement: Use pictures or text to answer a question about a historical topic.
Understand that history tells the story of people and events of other times and places.
Recognize examples of people and events from other times in stories.
Compare life now with life in the past.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, comparingschool, families, work, and community life.

standards.statement: Recognize examples of daily life that are different from long ago.
Identify celebrations and national holidays as a way of remembering and honoring past events, our nation's ethnic heritage, and the heroism and achievements of the people.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, federal holidays and ethnic celebrations.

standards.statement: Identify national holidays as a way of remembering and honoring people and events.
Identify people from the past who have shown character ideals and principles including honesty, courage, and responsibility.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,Presidents, war veterans, community members, and leaders.

standards.statement: Identify a person from the past who showed bravery, honesty, or responsibility.
Distinguish between historical fact and fiction using various materials.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to, tall tales, fables and non-fiction (expository) text.

standards.statement: Identify events or characters in a historical story that are real or not real.
Use terms related to time to sequentially order events that have occurred in school, home, or community.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,days, weeks, months, and years.

standards.statement: Recognize concepts of time related to a sequence of school events.
Create a timeline based on the student's life or school events, using primary sources.
standards.remarks: Examples of sourcesmay include, but are not limited to,photographs, birth certificates, report cards, and diaries.

standards.statement: Sequence three events in a student's life using photographs or pictures on a timeline.
Identify African American artists (i.e., Aretha Franklin, Charles White [Abraham Lincoln portrait artist], James Earl Jones, Maya Angelou).
Identify African American artists (i.e., Aretha Franklin, Charles White [Abraham Lincoln portrait], James Earl Jones, Maya Angelou).
Explain the purpose of rules and laws in the home, school, and community.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain the role that rules and laws play in their daily life. Clarification 2: Students will explain the difference between rules and laws.

standards.statement: Identify a rule and a law.
Describe how the absence of rules and laws impacts individuals and the community.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will provide examples of rules and laws in their lives and in the community. Clarification 2: Students will recognize that disorder, injustice, and harm to people can occur when there is an absence of rules and laws.

standards.statement: Recognize the effects of when rules or laws are not followed.
Explain the rights and responsibilities students have in the school community.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify the rights (e.g., treated with respect, physically safe learning environment) and responsibilities (e.g., come to school on time, do not damage school property) students have as members of their school community. Clarification 2: Students will define rights as freedoms protected by laws in society and protected by rules in the school community. Clarification 3: Students will define responsibilities as things citizens should do to benefit the community.

standards.statement: Identify responsibilities of students in a school community.
Describe the characteristics of citizenship in the school community.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify characteristics of responsible citizenship (e.g., respect others’ property, treat people with dignity, care for environment, treat animals with kindness). Clarification 2: Students will identify characteristics of irresponsible citizenship (e.g., damaging school property, bullying).

standards.statement: Identify characteristics of responsible citizenship in the school community.
Recognize ways citizens can demonstrate patriotism.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will discuss appropriate ways to show respect during the Pledge of Allegiance and National Anthem (e.g., stand at attention, face the flag, pause conversations). Clarification 2: Students will discuss how to show respect for the American flag (e.g., how to properly display and dispose of the American flag). Clarification 3: Students will discuss how to demonstrate patriotism during patriotic holidays and observances (e.g., American Founders Month, Celebrate Freedom Week, Constitution Day, Independence Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Medal of Honor Day, Memorial Day, Patriot Day, Veterans Day).

standards.statement: Identify ways citizens demonstrate patriotism during patriotic holidays.
Recognize symbols and individuals that represent the United States.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize the national motto, “In God We Trust” and the phrase, “We the People” as symbols that represent the United States. Clarification 2: Students will recognize Benjamin Franklin, George Washington, Daniel Webster, and Martin Luther King Jr. as individuals who represent the United States.

standards.statement: Identify the national motto "In God We Trust" as a symbol of the United States.
Recognize symbols and individuals that represent Florida.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize that the state motto (“In God We Trust”) and the state day (Pascua Florida Day) are symbols that represent Florida. Clarification 2: Students will identify the current Florida governor and recognize the governor as an individual who represents the state.

standards.statement: Identify the governor as an individual who represents the state of Florida.
Recognize that the United States and Florida have Constitutions.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will define a constitution as an agreed-upon set of rules or laws. Clarification 2: Students will recognize that the U.S. Constitution starts with “We the People.”

standards.statement: Identify a constitution as an agreed-upon set of rules.
Explain responsible ways for individuals and groups to make decisions.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will demonstrate characteristics of responsible decision-making. Clarification 2: Students will explain how multiple perspectives contribute to the unity of the United States.

standards.statement: Demonstrate ways of responsible decision-making such as voting on a class snack.
Recognize that money is used in the exchange of goods and services.
standards.remarks: An example is coins/bills versus bartering or trading.

standards.statement: Identify coins and bills as forms of money that can be used to buy things.
Define opportunity costs as giving up one thing for another.
standards.remarks: Examples are giving up television to do homework and buying candy versus saving for later purchase.

standards.statement: Recognize a situation that involves making a choice such as schoolwork or play.
Distinguish between examples of goods and services.
standards.remarks: Examples are goods: hamburger; services: sweeping the floor.

standards.statement: Recognize examples of goods and services.
Distinguish people as buyers, sellers, and producers of goods and services.
Recognize people who buy or sell goods.
Recognize the importance of saving money for future purchases.
Recognize ways to save money, such as putting it in a bank.
Identify that people need to make choices because of scarce resources.
standards.remarks: Examples are not enough time to do all activities or not enough red crayons.

standards.statement: Recognize when there is not enough of something (scarce resource).
Use physical, political, and cultural maps to locate places in Florida.
standards.remarks: Examples are Tallahassee, student's hometown, Lake Okeechobee, Florida Keys, and the Everglades.

standards.statement: Identify Florida and student's hometown on a map.
Identify key elements (i.e., compass rose, cardinal directions, title, key, or legend with symbols) of maps and globes.
Recognize key elements of maps and globes.
Construct a basic map using key elements including cardinal directions and map symbols.
standards.remarks: Examples are map of bedroom, classroom, or route to school

standards.statement: Complete a pictorial map using symbols for designated areas.
Identify a variety of physical features using a map and globe.
standards.remarks: Examples are oceans, peninsulas, lakes, rivers, swamps, and gulfs.

standards.statement: Identify land and water on a map and globe.
Locate on maps and globes the student’s local community, the state of Florida, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Gulf of America (formerly Gulf of Mexico).
Locate Florida and a major body of water that borders Florida.
Describe how location, weather, and physical environment affect the way people live in our community.
standards.remarks: Examples are effects on their food, clothing, shelter, transportation, and recreation

standards.statement: Identify a selected characteristic of the student's environment with its personal effect on the student.
Examine primary and secondary sources.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,artifacts, photographs, newspapers, audio/video recordings, documents, maps, coins, and stamps, textbooks and reference books.

standards.statement: Use primary and secondary sources to obtain information.
Utilize the media center, technology, or other informational sources to locate information that provides answers to questions about a historical topic.
Use technology and other informational sources to find answers to questions about a historical topic.
Recognize that Native Americans were the first inhabitants in North America.
Identify early Native Americans.
Compare the cultures of Native American tribes from various geographic regions of the United States.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,location, clothing, housing, food, major beliefs and practices, language, art, and music.

standards.statement: Identify practices of Native American tribes, such as clothing, housing, and food.
Describe the impact of immigrants on the Native Americans.
standards.remarks: Examples are location, clothing, housing, food, major beliefs and practices, art, and music.

standards.statement: Recognize the positive and negative impacts of immigrants on the Native Americans.
Explore ways the daily life of people living in Colonial America changed over time.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,food, shelter, clothing, education, and settlements.

standards.statement: Identify ways people living in colonial America changed their daily lives over time.
Identify reasons people came to the United States throughout history.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,war, hunger, natural disasters, voluntary and involuntary servitude, political or religious freedom, land, and jobs.

standards.statement: Recognize reasons why people came to the United States.
Discuss the importance of Ellis Island and the Statue of Liberty to immigration from 1892 - 1954.
Recognize Ellis Island as an immigration entry point to the United States from 1892-1954.
Discuss why immigration continues today.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to, jobs, war, hunger, natural disasters, politicalor religious freedom, and jobs.

standards.statement: Recognize reasons why people move to the United States today.
Explain the cultural influences and contributions of immigrants today.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to, food, language, music, art, beliefs and practices, literature, education, and clothing.

standards.statement: Recognize the cultural influences and contributions of immigrants today.
Identify terms and designations of time sequence.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,years, decades, centuries.

standards.statement: Identify concepts of time, including days, weeks, and months.
Identify African Americans who demonstrated civic service (i.e., Secretary of State Colin Powell, Civil Air Patrol [CAP] Lt. Willa Beatrice Brown, Carter G. Woodson, Senator Hiram Revels).
Identify an African American who demonstrated civic service (i.e., Secretary of State Colin Powell, Civil Air Patrol [CAP] Lt. Willa Beatrice Brown, Carter G. Woodson, Senator Hiram Revels).
Identify oral traditions and folktales of African Americans (e.g., Anansi the Spider, Tale of the Midnight Goat Thief).
Recognize an oral tradition or folktale of an African American (e.g., Anansi the Spider, Tale of the Midnight Goat Thief).
Explain why people form governments.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain the role of laws in government. Clarification 2: Students will define and provide examples of laws at the state and national levels. Clarification 3: Students will use scenarios to identify the impact of government on daily life.

standards.statement: Recognize the impact of local government on daily lives.
Explain how the U.S. government protects the liberty and rights of American citizens.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize that the equal rights of citizens are protected by the U.S. Constitution.

standards.statement: Identify a right protected by the U.S. Constitution.
Explain what it means to be a U.S. citizen.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize that there are multiple ways to obtain citizenship.

standards.statement: Recognize that individuals are born a U.S. citizen or can become one.
Describe the characteristics of responsible citizenship at the local and state levels.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify characteristics of responsible citizenship (e.g., peaceable assembly, obeying the law, community involvement). Clarification 2: Students will identify characteristics of irresponsible citizenship (e.g., disorderly assembly, breaking the law). Clarification 3: Students will describe the contributions of the diverse individuals and groups that contribute to civic life in the United States and Florida.

standards.statement: Recognize characteristics of responsible citizenship at the local level.
Explain how citizens demonstrate patriotism.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain why reciting the Pledge of Allegiance daily is an act of patriotism. Clarification 2: Students will explain the importance of recognizing patriotic holidays or observances (e.g., American Founders Month, Celebrate Freedom Week, Constitution Day, Independence Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Medal of Honor Day, Memorial Day, Patriot Day, Veterans Day).

standards.statement: Recognize that reciting the Pledge of Allegiance daily is an act of patriotism.
Recognize symbols, individuals, and documents that represent the United States.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize the U.S. Capitol, the White House, the U.S. Supreme Court building, and the Statue of Liberty as symbols that represent the United States. Clarification 2: Students will recognize Rosa Parks and Thomas Jefferson as individuals who represent the United States. Clarification 3: Students will recognize the Declaration of Independence as a document that represents the United States.

standards.statement: Identify documents that represent the United States.
Recognize symbols, individuals, and documents that represent Florida.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize the Florida State Capitol and the Everglades National Park as symbols of Florida. Clarification 2: Students will recognize Andrew Jackson and Marjory Stoneman Douglas as individuals who represent Florida. Clarification 3: Students will recognize the Florida Constitution as a document that represents Florida.

standards.statement: Identify symbols and individuals that represent Florida.
Identify the Constitution of the United States as the supreme law of the land.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize that the United States has a written constitution. Clarification 2: Students will identify the United States as a constitutional republic.

standards.statement: Recognize that the Constitution is the supreme law that all people must follow.
Recognize that people make choices because of limited resources.
Identify choices that people make with the availability of fewer resources.
Recognize that people supply goods and services based on consumer demands.
standards.remarks: Examples are housing and jobs.

standards.statement: Recognize that goods and services fill a need (demand).
Recognize that the United States trades with other nations to exchange goods and services.
standards.remarks: Examples are clothing, food, toys, cars.

standards.statement: Recognize that some goods come from other countries.
Explain the personal benefits and costs involved in saving and spending.
Identify a benefit of saving and spending.
Use different types of maps (political, physical, and thematic) to identify map elements.
standards.remarks: Examples are coordinate grids, title, compass rose, cardinal and intermediate directions, key/legend with symbols and scale.

standards.statement: Identify title, cardinal directions, and key/legend on a map.
Using maps and globes, locate the student’s hometown, Florida, North America, and both the state and national capitals.
Identify the student's hometown, Florida, and state capital on a map.
Label on a map or globe the continents, oceans, Equator, Prime Meridian, North and South Poles.
Recognize continents and oceans on a map or globe.
Use a map to locate the countries in North America (Canada, United States, Mexico, and the Caribbean Islands).
Recognize the United States on a map of North America.
Analyze primary and secondary sources.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,artifacts, photographs, paintings, maps, images, documents, audio and video recordings.

standards.statement: Identify and use primary and secondary sources to obtain information.
Utilize technology resources to gather information from primary and secondary sources.
Use technology resources to gather information about a primary or secondary source.
Define terms related to the social sciences.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,history, geography, civics, government, economics.

standards.statement: Recognize that the terms history, geography, economics, civics, and government are related to social sciences.

Identify African Americans who demonstrated heroism and patriotism (e.g., Booker T. Washington, Jesse Owens, Tuskegee Airmen, Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, President Barack Obama, 1st Lt. Vernon Baker, Sgt. 1st Class Melvin Morris).

Identify an African American who demonstrated heroism or patriotism (e.g., Booker T. Washington, Jesse Owens, Tuskegee Airmen, Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, President Barack Obama, 1st Lt. Vernon Baker, Sgt. 1st Class Melvin Morris).
Explain how the U.S. Constitution establishes the purpose and fulfills the need for government.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain the purpose of and need for government in terms of protection of rights, organization, security, and services.

standards.statement: Recognize the purpose of government in the community.
Describe how the U.S. government gains its power from the people.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize what is meant by “We the People” and the phrase, “consent of the governed.” Clarification 2: Students will identify sources of consent (e.g., voting and elections). Clarification 3: Students will recognize that the U.S. republic is governed by the “consent of the governed” and government power is exercised through representatives of the people.

standards.statement: Identify that government gains its power from the people.
Describe how citizens demonstrate civility, cooperation, volunteerism, and other civic virtues.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify examples including, but not limited to, food drives, book drives, community clean-ups, voting, blood donation drives, volunteer fire departments, and neighborhood watch programs.

standards.statement: Identify actions of citizens that contribute to the community.
Describe the importance of voting in elections.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize that it is every citizen’s responsibility to vote. Clarification 2: Students will explain the importance of voting in a republic.

standards.statement: Recognize that it is the responsibility of citizens to vote.
Explain the history and meaning behind patriotic holidays and observances.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify patriotic holidays and observances to include, but not limited to, American Founders Month, Celebrate Freedom Week, Constitution Day, Independence Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Medal of Honor Day, Memorial Day, Patriot Day, and Veterans Day.

standards.statement: Recognize the meaning behind patriotic holidays.
Recognize symbols, individuals, documents, and events that represent the United States.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize Mount Rushmore, Uncle Sam, and the Washington Monument as symbols that represent the United States. Clarification 2: Students will recognize James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, Booker T. Washington, and Susan B. Anthony as individuals who represent the United States. Clarification 3: Students will recognize the U.S. Constitution as a document that represents the United States. Clarification 4: Students will recognize the Constitutional Convention (May 1787 – September 1787) and the signing of the U.S. Constitution (September 17, 1787) as events that represent the United States.

standards.statement: Identify events that represent the United States.
Recognize symbols, individuals, documents, and events that represent the State of Florida.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize the Great Seal of the State of Florida as a symbol that represents the state. Clarification 2: Students will recognize William Pope Duval, William Dunn Moseley, and Josiah T. Walls as individuals who represent Florida. Clarification 3: Students will identify the Declaration of Rights in the Florida Constitution as a document that represents Florida. Clarification 4: Students will recognize that Florida became the 27th state of the United States on March 3, 1845.

standards.statement: Identify events that represent Florida.
Explain how the U.S. and Florida Constitutions establish the structure, function, powers, and limits of government.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize that the U.S. Constitution and the Florida Constitution establish the framework for national and state government. Clarification 2: Students will recognize how government is organized at the national level (e.g., three branches of government). Clarification 3: Students will provide examples of people who make and enforce rules and laws in the United States (e.g., congress and president) and Florida (e.g., state legislature and governor).

standards.statement: Identify that the U.S. and Florida Constitutions have three branches of government.
Recognize that government has local, state, and national levels.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize that each level of government has its own unique structure and responsibilities. Clarification 2: Students will distinguish between the responsibilities of the local, state, and national governments in the United States.

standards.statement: Identify levels of local, state, and federal government to their functions.
Give examples of how scarcity results in trade.
standards.remarks: Examples are oil, video games, food.

standards.statement: Recognize that people can trade for products that are not available locally.
List the characteristics of money.
standards.remarks: Examples are portable, divisible, recognizable, durable.

standards.statement: Identify some characteristics of money.
Recognize that buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods and services through the use of trade or money.
Recognize the roles of buyers and sellers in exchanging goods and services.
Distinguish between currencies used in the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
Recognize forms of money used in the United States and one other North American country
Use thematic maps, tables, charts, graphs, and photos to analyze geographic information.
standards.remarks: Types of photographs may include satellite or aerial.

standards.statement: Use a thematic map or chart to identify selected geographic information, such as land and body of water on a map or population on a chart.
Review basic map elements (coordinate grid, cardinal and intermediate directions, title, compass rose, scale, key or legend with symbols).
Identify elements on a map, such as title, key/legend, cardinal directions, compass rose, and coordinate grid.
Label the continents and oceans on a world map.
Identify selected continents and oceans on a world map.
Name and identify the purpose of maps (physical, political, elevation, population).
Recognize a physical and a political map.
Compare maps and globes to develop an understanding of the concept of distortion.
Identify differences between maps and globes.
Use maps to identify different types of scale to measure distances between two places.
standards.remarks: Examples are linear, fractional, word.

standards.statement: Use maps to identify distances between two places.
Label the countries and commonwealths in North America (Canada, United States, Mexico) and in the Caribbean (Puerto Rico, Cuba, Bahamas, Dominican Republic, Haiti, Jamaica).
Recognize North America as Canada, the United States, and Mexico on a map.
Identify the five regions of the United States.
standards.remarks: (i.e., Northeast, Southeast, Midwest, Southwest, West)

standards.statement: Recognize north, south, east, and west as they relate to the regions of the United States.
Label the states in each of the five regions of the United States.
Recognize selected states in each of the five regions of the United States.
Describe the physical features of the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
standards.remarks: Examples are lakes, rivers, oceans, mountains, deserts, plains, and grasslands.

standards.statement: Recognize major physical features of the United States, Canada, and Mexico.
Identify natural and man-made landmarks in the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
standards.remarks: (e.g. Grand Canyon, Gateway Arch, Mount Rushmore, Devil's Tower, Mt. Denali, Everglades, Niagara Falls)

standards.statement: Recognize major natural and man-made landmarks of the United States.
Investigate how people perceive places and regions differently by conducting interviews, mental mapping and studying news, poems, legends, and songs about a region or area.
Identify how people view places and regions differently by asking questions about a region.
Describe the climate and vegetation in the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
standards.remarks: (e.g., tundra, sandy soil, humidity, maritime climate)

standards.statement: Recognize differences in the climates of the United States, Canada, and Mexico.
Describe the natural resources in the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
standards.remarks: (e.g., water, arable land, oil, phosphate, fish)

standards.statement: Recognize major natural resources in the United States, Canada, and Mexico.
Explain how the environment influences settlement patterns in the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
standards.remarks: Examples are settlements near water for drinking, bathing, cooking, agriculture and land for farming.

standards.statement: Identify major ways environmental influences contribute to settlement patterns in the United States.
Identify the cultures that have settled the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
Recognize different cultures that have settled in the United States.
Compare the cultural characteristics of diverse populations in one of the five regions of the United States with Canada, Mexico, or the Caribbean.
standards.remarks: Examples are housing, music, transportation, food, recreation, language, holidays, beliefs and customs.

standards.statement: Identify a cultural characteristic of a population in the United States and a population in Mexico or Canada.
Identify contributions from various ethnic groups to the United States.
standards.remarks: Examples are Native Americans, Hispanics/Latinos, Africans, Asians, Europeans.

standards.statement: Recognize contributions of an ethnic group to the United States.
Analyze primary and secondary resources to identify significant individuals and events throughout Florida history.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to, photographs, paintings, maps, artifacts, timelines, audio and video, letters and diaries, periodicals, newspaper articles, etc.

standards.statement: Identify and use primary and secondary resources to obtain information related to Florida history.
Synthesize information related to Florida history through print and electronic media.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to, encyclopedias, atlases, newspapers, websites, databases, audio, video, etc.

standards.statement: Use print and electronic media to collect information about Florida history.
Compare Native American tribes in Florida.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,Apalachee, Calusa, Tequesta, Timucua, Tocobaga.

standards.statement: Identify important cultural aspects of Native American tribes of Florida.
Identify explorers who came to Florida and the motivations for their expeditions.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,Ponce de Leon, Juan Garrido, Esteban Dorantes, Tristan deLuna, and an understanding that 2013 is the quincentennial of the founding of Florida.

standards.statement: Recognize a European explorer who came to Florida.
Describe causes and effects of European colonization on the Native American tribes of Florida.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, protection of ships, search for gold, glory of the mother country, disease, death, and spread of religion.

standards.statement: Identify effects of European colonization on Native American tribes in Florida.
Identify the significance of St. Augustine as the oldest permanent European settlement in the United States.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, the 450th anniversary of the founding of St. Augustine in 2015 as the first continuous town in the United States, predating other colonial settlements.

standards.statement: Recognize St. Augustine as the beginning of Spanish colonial settlement in the United States.
Explain the purpose of and daily life on missions (San Luis de Talimali in present-day Tallahassee).
Identify a purpose of missions in Florida.
Identify the significance of Fort Mose as the first free African community in the United States.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, the differences between Spanish and English treatment of enslavement.

standards.statement: Identify Fort Mose as the first free African community in the United States.
Identify the effects of Spanish rule in Florida.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to, names of cities such as Pensacola, etc., agriculture, weapons, architecture, art, music, and food.

standards.statement: Recognize effects of Spanish rule in early Florida.
Identify nations (Spain, France, England) that controlled Florida before it became a United States territory.
Identify a different nation that controlled Florida.
Explain how the Seminole tribe formed and the purpose for their migration.
Identify one reason why the Seminole tribe was formed and where they lived.
Explain how Florida (Adams-Onis Treaty) became a U.S. territory.
Recognize that Spain gave Florida back to the United States.
Identify the causes and effects of the Seminole Wars.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, Jackson's invasion of Florida (First Seminole War), without federal permission.

standards.statement: Recognize that the United States fought wars against the Seminole tribe.
Explain the effects of technological advances on Florida.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, steam engine, steamboats, delivery of water to some areas of the state.

standards.statement: Identify technological advances that helped Florida to grow.
Describe pioneer life in Florida.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, butare not limited to, therole of men, women, children, Florida Crackers, Black Seminoles.

standards.statement: Identify characteristics of pioneer life in Florida.
Describe Florida's involvement (secession, blockades of ports, the battles of Ft. Pickens, Olustee, Ft. Brooke, Natural Bridge, food supply) in the Civil War.
standards.remarks: Additional examples may also include, but are not limited to, Ft. Zachary Taylor, the plantation culture, the First Florida Cavalry.

standards.statement: Recognize that Florida was considered a slave state (South) and battles were fought in Florida during the Civil War.
Summarize challenges Floridians faced during Reconstruction.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,sharecropping, segregation, and black participation in state and federal governments.

standards.statement: Recognize the effects of Reconstruction in Florida.
Describe the economic development of Florida's major industries.
standards.remarks: Examplesof industries may include, but are not limited to, timber, citrus, cattle, tourism, phosphate, cigar, railroads, bridges, air conditioning, sponge, shrimping, and wrecking (pirating).

standards.statement: Recognize Florida's major industries.
Summarize contributions immigrant groups made to Florida.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,language, food, art, beliefs and practices, literature, education, and clothing.

standards.statement: Identify contributions of immigrants to Florida.
Describe the contributions of significant individuals to Florida.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,John Gorrie, Henry Flagler, Henry Plant, Lue Gim Gong, Vincente Martinez Ybor, Julia Tuttle, Mary McLeod Bethune, Thomas Alva Edison, James Weldon Johnson, Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings.

standards.statement: Identify the contributions of significant individuals to Florida.
Describe effects of the Spanish American War on Florida.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to, cigar industry, temporary economic boom at Ft. Brooke due to Rough Riders, Cuban immigration.

standards.statement: Recognize ways that Florida changed during the Spanish American War.
Describe the causes and effects of the 1920's Florida land boom and bust.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, land speculation.

standards.statement: Identify a basic cause and effect of the 1920s Florida land boom and bust.
Summarize challenges Floridians faced during the Great Depression.
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, the Labor Day hurricane of 1935 and the Mediterranean fruit fly.

standards.statement: Identify a challenge Floridians faced during the Great Depression.
Identify Florida’s role in World War II.
Identify Florida's role in the Civil Rights Movement.
standards.remarks: Examplesmay include, but are not limited to,Tallahassee Bus Boycotts, civil disobedience, and the legacy of early civil rights pioneers, Harry T. and Harriette V. Moore.

standards.statement: Recognize that Florida played a role in the Civil Rights Movement.
Describe how and why immigration impacts Florida today.
Identify how immigration impacts Florida today.
Describe the effect of the United States' space program on Florida's economy and growth.
Recognize an impact the space program has on Florida's growth.
Explain how tourism affects Florida's economy and growth.
Recognize that tourism brings people and money to Florida.
Utilize timelines to sequence key events in Florida history.
Complete a timeline to sequence major events in Florida history.

Identify African American community leaders who made positive contributions in the state of Florida (e.g., Zora Neale Hurston, Florida Highwaymen, Mary McLeod Bethune, Evan B. Forde, Bessie Coleman, Gen. Daniel “Chappie” James, Bob Hayes, Sylvia Fowles).

Identify an African American community leader who made positive contributions in the state of Florida (e.g., Zora Neale Hurston, Florida Highwaymen, Mary McLeod Bethune, Evan B. Forde, Bessie Coleman, Gen. Daniel "Chappie" James, Bob Hayes, Sylvia Fowles).
Explain why the Florida government has a written Constitution.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize that every state has a state constitution. Clarification 2: Students will explain the relationship between a written constitution, the government established, and the citizens.

standards.statement: Recognize that Florida's constitution protects the rights of Florida's citizens and identifies the parts and functions of state government.
Identify and describe how citizens work with local and state governments to solve problems.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain how public issues, such as taxation, roads, zoning, and schools, impact citizens’ daily lives. Clarification 2: Students will describe how citizens can help solve community and state problems (e.g., attending government meetings, communicating with their elected representatives).

standards.statement: Recognize how citizens work with government to solve community problems.
Explain the importance of voting, public service, and volunteerism to the state and nation.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain how voting, public service, and volunteerism contribute to the preservation of the republic. Clarification 2: Students will discuss different types of public service and volunteerism.

standards.statement: Identify different types of public service and volunteerism.
Identify individuals who represent the citizens of Florida at the state level.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify their local state senator and state representative. Clarification 2: Students will identify appropriate methods for communicating with elected officials. Clarification 3: Students will recognize that Florida has a representative government.

standards.statement: Recognize that Florida has a representative government.
Explain the structure and functions of the legislative, executive, and judicial branches of government in Florida.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will compare the powers of Florida’s three branches of government. Clarification 2: Students will explain how the Declaration of Rights in the Florida Constitution protects the rights of citizens.

standards.statement: Recognize Florida's three branches of government, including legislative (makes laws), judicial (interprets laws), and executive (enforces laws).
Compare the structure, functions, and processes of local and state government.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify how government is organized at the local and state level including, but not limited to, legislative branch (e.g., legislature, city/county commission), executive branch (e.g., governor, mayor) and judicial branch (e.g., county and circuit courts).

standards.statement: Identify the structures of local and state governments.
Identify entrepreneurs from various social and ethnic backgrounds who have influenced Florida and local economy.
standards.remarks: Examples are Henry Flagler, Walt Disney, Ed Ball, Alfred Dupont, Julia Tuttle, Vincente Martinez Ybor.

standards.statement: Recognize a contribution of an entrepreneur who influenced Florida.
Explain Florida's role in the national and international economy and conditions that attract businesses to the state.
standards.remarks: Examples are tourism, agriculture, phosphate, space industry.

standards.statement: Identify important economic contributions of Florida.
People have many different types of jobs from which to choose. Identify different jobs requiring people to have different skills.
standards.remarks: Make a list of different types of jobs and describe the different skills associated with each job.

standards.statement: Identify different skills with different types of jobs.
People earn an income when they are hired by an employer to work at a job. Explain why employers are willing to pay people to do their work.
Recognize that people get paid for their work.
Workers are paid for their labor in different ways such as wages, salaries, or commissions. Explain the ways in which workers are paid.
standards.examples: Explain how a waitress, a teacher, and a realtor are paid.

standards.statement: Recognize that workers are paid in different ways for different jobs.
People can earn interest income from letting other people borrow their money. Explain why banks and financial institutions pay people interest when they deposit their money at those institutions.
Identify interest income from people borrowing money.
People can earn income by renting their property to other people. Identify different types of property (such as apartments, automobiles, or tools) that people own and on which rent is paid.
Recognize income can be earned by renting to others.
Describe ways that people who own a business can earn a profit, which is a source of income.
Recognize that people who own a business can make money.

Entrepreneurs are people who start new businesses. Entrepreneurs do not know if their new businesses will be successful and earn a profit. Identify ways in which starting a business is risky for entrepreneurs.
standards.remarks: Read a children’s book about an entrepreneur and identify the type of business started, the possible risks of running the business, and what the entrepreneur expected to earn.

standards.statement: Recognize that entrepreneurs are people who start new businesses.
Income earned from working and most other sources of income are taxed. Describe ways that the revenue from these taxes is used to pay for government provided goods and services.
standards.remarks: Describe examples of government-provided goods and services that are paid for with taxes.

standards.statement: Recognize taxes are used to pay for government goods and services.
Explain that economic wants are desires that can be satisfied by consuming a good, a service, or a leisure activity.
standards.remarks: Brainstorm a list of wants and then identify examples of goods, services, or leisure activities they can buy to satisfy each want.

standards.statement: Identify economic wants with goods, services, and leisure activities.
Explain that people make choices about what goods and services they buy because they can’t have everything they want. This requires individuals to prioritize their wants.
standards.remarks: Create a list of goods or services they want given a set budget constraint, rank the goods and services from the most to the least desired, and justify their ranking.

standards.statement: Place goods and services in a list that prioritizes an individual's wants.
Identify some of the ways that people spend a portion of their income on goods and services in order to increase their personal satisfaction or happiness.
standards.remarks: Explain why consumers with identical vacation budgets choose different options when planning a weeklong vacation.

standards.statement: Recognize a portion of income can be used for personal happiness.
Discuss that whenever people buy something, they incur an opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a person makes a choice.
standards.remarks: Present an example of a buying choice a person made and identify the opportunity cost of that choice.

standards.statement: Recognize a scenario that involves making an economic choice.
Explain that costs are things that a decision maker gives up; benefits are things that a decision maker gains. Make an informed decision by comparing the costs and benefits of spending alternatives.
standards.remarks: Compare the costs and benefits of buying a bicycle in two settings, rural and urban, and for different people including a younger child, a teenager, and a grandparent.

standards.statement: Identify the costs and benefits of spending based on an informed decision.
Predict how people’s spending choices are influenced by prices as well as many other factors, including advertising, the spending choices of others, and peer pressure.
standards.remarks: Write stories about how individual spending choices were informed or influenced by advertising, the spending choices of others, peer pressure, or the prices of alternative choices. Explain why shopping with a list can help consumers with their spending choices.

standards.statement: Identify ways people's spending choices are influenced.
Planning for spending can help people make informed choices. Develop a budget plan for spending, saving, and managing income.
standards.remarks: Create a budget for a set amount of allowance income that includes expenses (buying of goods and services) and savings.

standards.statement: Identify the parts of a budget plan (spending, saving, and managing income).
Identify ways that income is saved, spent on goods and services, or used to pay taxes.
standards.remarks: Explain the difference between saving and spending and give examples of each.

standards.statement: Recognize ways that income is used.
Explain that when people save money, they give up the opportunity to buy things now in order to buy things later.
standards.remarks: Describe what a person gives up when he or she deposits $20 into a savings account.

standards.statement: Recognize that saving money involves choices
Identify ways that people can choose to save money in many places—for example, at home in a piggy bank or at a commercial bank, credit union, or savings and loan.
standards.remarks: Draw a picture identifying the different places where people can save their money.

standards.statement: Identify places where people can save money.
Identify savings goals people set as incentives to save. One savings goal might be to buy goods and services in the future.
standards.remarks: Read a children’s book and identify a character’s savings goal and whether the character meets the savings goal.

standards.statement: Identify the relationship between saving money and future purchases.

Explain that when people deposit money into a bank (or other financial institution), the bank may pay them interest. Banks attract savings by paying interest. People also deposit money into banks because banks are safe places to keep their savings.
standards.remarks: Describe the advantages of saving money in a savings account rather than putting the money into a piggy bank.

standards.statement: Recognize the advantages of saving money in a bank.
Discuss that interest is the price the borrower pays for using someone else’s money.
standards.remarks: Explain the reason why, when a person borrows $100 to buy a new cell phone, he or she will have to pay back more than the $100 at a future date.

standards.statement: Recognize that interest is added when you borrow money.
Identify instances when people use credit, that they receive something of value now and agree to repay the lender over time, or at some date in the future, with interest.
standards.remarks: Identify goods and services people often purchase with the use of a loan.

standards.statement: Identify an instance when people use a loan.
Explain that after people have saved some of their income, they must decide how to invest their savings so that it can grow over time.
standards.remarks: Describe the difference between saving and financial investing.

standards.statement: Recognize the difference between saving and financial investing.
Explain that a financial investment is the purchase of a financial asset, such as a stock, with the expectation of an increase in the value of the asset and/or increase in future income.
standards.remarks: Explain why a stockholder may benefit if the company produces an increasingly popular product.

standards.statement: Recognize that an investment may or may not produce a future income.
Explain that risk is the chance of loss or harm.
standards.remarks: Give examples of the risk associated with activities such as riding a bicycle, using a skateboard, or having a pet.

standards.statement: Recognize common examples of a risk.
Explain that risk from accidents and unexpected events is an unavoidable part of daily life.
standards.remarks: Write a newspaper article on an unexpected “bad” event such as a tornado, car accident, or illness, and describe the effect the event would have on individuals and their families.

standards.statement: Recognize that unexpected events are part of daily life.
Describe ways that individuals can either choose to accept risk or take steps to protect themselves by avoiding or reducing risk.
standards.remarks: Draw a poster depicting an age-appropriate activity (e.g., owning and riding a bicycle) that illustrates how to avoid risk of harm or loss (not riding the bike) or how to reduce the chance of a bad event (riding in a safe manner) and potential harm of the bad event (wearing a bike helmet).

standards.statement: Identify ways to avoid or reduce risks.
Discuss that one method to cope with unexpected losses is to save for emergencies.
standards.remarks: Give examples of events for which emergency savings could offset financial losses.

standards.statement: Recognize a benefit of emergency savings.
Identify physical features of Florida.
standards.remarks: Examples are bodies of water, location, landforms.

standards.statement: Recognize selected physical features of Florida.
Locate and label cultural features on a Florida map.
standards.remarks: Examples are state capitals, major cities, tourist attractions.

standards.statement: Identify cultural features on a Florida map.
Explain how weather impacts Florida.
standards.remarks: Examples are hurricanes, thunderstorms, drought, mild climate.

standards.statement: Recognize an effect of weather in Florida.
Interpret political and physical maps using map elements (title, compass rose, cardinal directions, intermediate directions, symbols, legend, scale, longitude, latitude).
Identify information provided on maps using the title, compass rose, cardinal and intermediate directions, symbols, and key/legend.
Use primary and secondary sources to understand history.
Use primary and secondary resources to understand history.
Utilize timelines to identify and discuss American History time periods.
Sequence events to match dates on a timeline about American history.
Compare cultural aspects of ancient American civilizations (e.g., Aztecs, Mayas, Mound Builders, Anasazi, Inuit).
standards.remarks: Examples may include, but are not limited to, those listed in the benchmark.

standards.statement: Recognize a cultural aspect of an ancient North American civilization.

Identify Native American tribes from different geographic regions of North America (cliff dwellers and Pueblo people of the desert Southwest, coastal tribes of the Pacific Northwest, nomadic nations of the Great Plains, woodland tribes east of the Mississippi River).
Recognize that Native American tribes lived in various parts of North America and had different customs.

Compare cultural aspects of Native American tribes from different geographic regions of North America including but not limited to clothing, shelter, food, major beliefs and practices, music, art, and interactions with the environment.
Recognize differences in cultural aspects of Native American tribes.
Describe technological developments that shaped European exploration.
Recognize inventions that made exploration safer.
Investigate (nationality, sponsoring country, motives, dates and routes of travel, accomplishments) the European explorers.
Identify a European explorer with their sponsoring country.
Describe interactions among Native Americans, Africans, English, French, Dutch, and Spanish for control of North America.
Recognize ways different groups interacted with each other for control of North America.
Identify the economic, political and socio-cultural motivation for colonial settlement.
Recognize reasons why colonists settled in America.
Compare characteristics of New England, Middle, and Southern colonies.
Identify resources found in a colonial region.
Identify significant individuals responsible for the development of the New England, Middle, and Southern colonies.
Identify an individual responsible for the development of new colonies.
Demonstrate an understanding of political, economic, and social aspects of daily colonial life in the thirteen colonies.
Recognize aspects of daily colonial life.
Explain the importance of Triangular Trade linking Africa, the West Indies, the British Colonies, and Europe.
Identify the Triangular Trade with slavery.
Describe the introduction, impact, and role of slavery in the colonies.
Recognize that Southern Colonies had large farms with slaves.
Identify and explain significant events leading up to the American Revolution.
Identify events that led up to the American Revolution.
Identify significant individuals and groups who played a role in the American Revolution.
Identify a significant individual who contributed to the American Revolution.
Explain the significance of historical documents including key political concepts, origins of these concepts, and their role in American independence.
Identify that the Declaration of Independence stated that colonists wanted freedom from England.
Examine and explain the changing roles and impact of significant women during the American Revolution.
Identify a significant woman from the American Revolution.
Examine and compare major battles and military campaigns of the American Revolution.
Recognize a major battle in the American Revolution.
Identify the contributions of foreign alliances and individuals to the outcome of the Revolution.
Recognize that the colonies needed help from other countries to win the American Revolution.
Explain economic, military, and political factors which led to the end of the Revolutionary War.
Identify factors that helped colonists win the Revolution.
Evaluate the personal and political hardships resulting from the American Revolution.
Recognize that the colonists needed more money and supplies after the American Revolution.
Discuss the impact and significance of land policies developed under the Confederation Congress (Northwest Ordinance of 1787).
Recognize that the United States wanted to add new land after the Revolution.
Examine the significance of the Constitution including its key political concepts, origins of those concepts, and their role in American democracy.
Recognize that the Constitution outlines the principles of the American government.
Describe the causes and effects of the Louisiana Purchase.
Recognize that the Louisiana Purchase made the United States twice its original size.
Identify roles and contributions of significant people during the period of westward expansion.
Recognize significant people in the westward expansion of the United States.
Examine 19th century advancements (canals, roads, steamboats, flat boats, overland wagons, Pony Express, railroads) in transportation and communication.
Identify an advancement with transportation and communication in America during the 1800s.
Explain the importance of the explorations west of the Mississippi River.
Recognize significant exploration achievements west of the Mississippi River.
Identify the causes and effects of the War of 1812.
Recognize that America fought England in the War of 1812.
Explain how westward expansion affected Native Americans.
Recognize the westward expansion impacted Native Americans.
Discuss the concept of Manifest Destiny.
Identify Manifest Destiny with westward expansion.
Describe the causes and effects of the Missouri Compromise.
Identify one cause and one effect of the Missouri Compromise.
Describe the hardships of settlers along the overland trails to the west.
Identify hardships settlers faced as they moved west.
Examine the life of African Americans in the colonial era.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Instruction includes what life was like for the earliest slaves and the emancipated in North America.

standards.statement: Recognize how African Americans lived in the colonial era.
Examine the Underground Railroad and how former slaves partnered with other free people and groups in assisting those escaping from slavery.
Recognize the purpose of the Underground Railroad in assisting those escaping from slavery.
Examine key figures and events in abolitionist movements.
Recognize the purpose of the Underground Railroad in assisting those escaping from slavery.
Identify freedoms and rights secured for and by former slaves.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Instruction will include the Emancipation Proclamation, 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments to the Constitution of the United States.

standards.statement: Recognize a freedom or right secured for and by former slaves.
Examine the roles and contributions of significant African Americans during westward expansion (e.g., Benjamin “Pap” Singleton, James Beckwourth, Buffalo Soldiers, York [American explorer]).
Recognize the importance of an African American during the westward expansion (e.g., Benjamin "Pap" Singleton, James Beckwourth, Buffalo Soldiers, York [American explorer]).
Examine the experiences and contributions of African Americans in early Florida.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Instruction includes African American communities (e.g., Fort Mose, Angola Community, Black Seminoles, Fort Gadsden, Lincolnville, Eatonville).

standards.statement: Recognize an experience or contribution of African Americans in early Florida.
Recognize that the Declaration of Independence affirms that every U.S. citizen has certain unalienable rights.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify the grievances detailed in the Declaration of Independence. Clarification 2: Students will describe the idea of “unalienable rights” in the Declaration of Independence as it relates to each citizen. Clarification 3: Students will discuss the consequences of governments not recognizing that citizens have certain unalienable rights.

standards.statement: Identify the idea of "unalienable rights" in the Declaration of Independence as it relates to each citizen.
Explain how and why the U.S. government was created by the U.S. Constitution.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify the strengths and weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation. Clarification 2: Students will explain the goals of the 1787 Constitutional Convention. Clarification 3: Students will describe why compromises were made during the writing of the Constitution and identify those compromises (e.g., Great Compromise, the Three-Fifths Compromise, the Electoral College). Clarification 4: Students will identify Federalist and Anti-Federalist arguments supporting and opposing the ratification of the U.S. Constitution.

standards.statement: Recognize a compromise that was made during the writing of the Constitution.
Discuss arguments for adopting a representative form of government.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain what is meant by a representative government.

standards.statement: Recognize the United States is a representative government.
Describe the history, meaning, and significance of the Bill of Rights.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will describe how concerns about individual rights led to the inclusion of the Bill of Rights in the U.S. Constitution.

standards.statement: Recognize the significance of the Bill of Rights in the U.S. Constitution.
Discuss the political ideas of Patriots, Loyalists, and other colonists about the American Revolution.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will describe the political philosophy of American Patriots and why those ideas led them to declare independence from the British Empire. Clarification 2: Students will explain why colonists would choose to side with the British during the American Revolution. Clarification 3: Students will examine motivations for the decision to not take a side during the American Revolution.

standards.statement: Identify political ideas of Patriots and Loyalists.
Compare forms of political participation in the colonial period to today.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will describe forms of political participation in the colonial period (e.g., serving on juries, militia service, participation in elections for government). Clarification 2: Students will identify ways citizens participate in the political process today (e.g., serving on juries, participation in elections for government).

standards.statement: Recognize ways citizens participate in the political process historically and in modern times.
Analyze how the U.S. Constitution expanded civic participation over time.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will describe how the U.S. Constitution expanded voting rights through amendments and legislation including, but not limited to, the 15th, 19th, 24th, and 26th Amendments, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

standards.statement: Recognize voting rights within the U.S. Constitution.
Evaluate the importance of civic duties and responsibilities to the preservation of the United States’ constitutional republic.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain what it means for the United States to be a constitutional republic. Clarification 2: Students will identify duties (e.g., obeying the law, paying taxes, serving on a jury) and responsibilities (e.g., voting, keeping informed on public issues) that citizens are expected to fulfill. Clarification 3: Students will explain what could happen to the United States if citizens did not fulfill their civic duties and responsibilities.

standards.statement: Recognize duties and responsibilities that citizens are expected to fulfill.
Identify individuals who represent the citizens of Florida at the national level.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify Florida’s U.S. senators and the U.S. representative for their district. Clarification 2: Students will discuss the constitutional qualifications for office, term length, authority, duties, activities, and compensation.

standards.statement: Recognize Florida's U.S. senators and representatives from their district.
Explain symbols and documents that represent the United States.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize the Great Seal of the United States and the Star-Spangled Banner as symbols that represent the United States. Clarification 2: Students will recognize the U.S. Constitution (specifically the Bill of Rights) and the Emancipation Proclamation as documents that represent the United States.

standards.statement: Identify a symbol and a document that represents the United States.
Describe the organizational structure and powers of the national government as defined in Articles I, II, and III of the U.S. Constitution.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will identify legislative, executive, and judicial branch functions of the U.S. government as defined in Articles I, II, and III of the U.S. Constitution. Clarification 2: Students will explain why the Constitution divides the national government into three branches.

standards.statement: Recognize the structure of the national government as defined in the U.S. Constitution.
Analyze how the U.S. Constitution and Bill of Rights limit the power of the national government and protect citizens from an oppressive government.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will recognize examples of what to include, but not be limited to, popular sovereignty, rule of law, separation of powers, checks and balances, federalism, the amendment process, and the fundamental rights of citizens in the Bill of Rights.

standards.statement: Recognize that the power of the national government is limited by the U.S. Constitution and the Bill of Rights.
Explain the role of the court system in interpreting law and settling conflicts.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain why the U.S. Supreme Court is the highest court in the system. Clarification 2: Students will explain why both the United States and Florida have a Supreme Court.

standards.statement: Recognize the role of the United States and Florida Supreme Court.
Describe the process for amending the U.S. Constitution.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will explain why the U.S. Constitution includes the amendment process. Clarification 2: Students will identify amendments to the U.S. Constitution.

standards.statement: Recognize that the U.S. Constitution has amendments.
Explain how the U.S. Constitution influenced the Florida Constitution.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1 : Students will identify the purpose of a constitution (e.g., provides a framework for government, limits government authority, protects the rights of the people). Clarification 2 : Students will recognize the basic outline of the U.S. and Florida Constitutions (both have articles, amendments, and preambles).

standards.statement: Recognize the basic outline of the U.S. and Florida Constitutions.
Explain the relationship between the state and national governments.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will define federalism as it applies to the United States. Clarification 2: Students will provide examples of powers granted to the national government and those reserved to the states. Clarification 3: Students will provide examples of cooperation between the U.S. and Florida governments.

standards.statement: Identify examples of powers granted to the national government and those reserved to the states.
Identify how trade promoted economic growth in North America from pre-Columbian times to 1850.
Recognize how trade promoted growth in pre-Columbian times to 1850.
Describe a market economy, and give examples of how the colonial and early American economy exhibited these characteristics.
Identify a characteristic of a market economy in colonial America.
Trace the development of technology and the impact of major inventions on business productivity during the early development of the United States.
Recognize major inventions during the early development of the United States.
Recognize the positive and negative effects of voluntary trade among Native Americans, European explorers, and colonists.
Recognize a positive and a negative effect of voluntary trade in early America.
Interpret current and historical information using a variety of geographic tools.
Recognize current and historical information using selected geographic tools.
Use latitude and longitude to locate places.
Use a coordinate grid on a map to locate places.
Identify major United States physical features on a map of North America.
Recognize major physical features on a map of the United States.
Construct maps, charts, and graphs to display geographic information.
Complete a map, chart, or graph to display geographic information.
Identify and locate the original thirteen colonies on a map of North America.
Identify an original colony on a map of the United States.
Locate and identify states, capitals, and United States Territories on a map.
Identify selected states and their capitals on a map.
Describe the push-pull factors (economy, natural hazards, tourism, climate, physical features) that influenced boundary changes within the United States.
Identify a factor that causes a boundary to change.
Describe the impact that past natural events have had on human and physical environments in the United States through 1850.
Identify natural events that caused change through the 1850s.
Use geographic knowledge and skills when discussing current events.
Use a geographic skill to recognize information about current events.
Use geography concepts and skills such as recognizing patterns, mapping, and graphing to find solutions for local, state, or national problems.
Use a geographic skill to recognize information about selected local, state, or national events.
Define the Holocaust as the planned and systematic state-sponsored persecution and murder of European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1933 and 1945.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Students will define antisemitism as prejudice against or hatred of the Jewish people. Clarification 2: Students will recognize the Holocaust as history’s most extreme example of antisemitism. Clarification3: Students will identify examples of antisemitism (e.g., calling for, aiding, or justifying the killing or harming of Jews).

standards.statement: Recognize the Holocaust as history's most extreme example of antisemitism.
Identify Afro-Eurasian trade routes and methods prior to the development of the Atlantic slave trade.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Instruction includes how slavery was utilized in Asian, European, and African cultures. Clarification 2: Instruction includes the similarities and differences between serfdom and slavery. Clarification 3: Instruction includes the use of maps to identify trade routes.

standards.statement: Recognize trade routes between Africa, Europe and Asia before the Atlantic slave trade started.
Describe the contact of European explorers with systematic slave trading in Africa.
Recognize how European explorers were connected to the slave trade in Africa.
Examine the evolution of the labor force in the use of indentured servitude contracts.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Instruction includes the comparative treatment of indentured servants of European and African extraction. Clarification 2: Instruction includes the transition from an indentured to a slave-based economy.

standards.statement: Recognize how the labor force has changed over time for indentured servants.
Describe the history and evolution of slave codes.
standards.clarifications: Clarification 1: Instruction includes judicial and legislative actions concerning slavery.

standards.statement: Recognize the history and changes of slave codes.
Analyze slave revolts that happened in early colonial America and how political leaders reacted (e.g., 1712 revolt in New York City, Stono Rebellion [1739]).
Recognize how enslaved people resisted slavery and how leaders reacted in early colonial America (e.g., 1712 revolt in New York City, Stono Rebellion [1739]).
Examine the service and sacrifice of African patriots during the Revolutionary Era (e.g., Crispus Attucks, Peter Salem, James Armistead Lafayette, 1st Rhode Island Regiment).
